contracts.name: TheDAO
contracts.purpose: A simplified model of The DAO, a token-based investment pool. Users deposit ether to mint tokens 1:1, can transfer tokens, and can add profit to a reward pool shared among holders. A holder exits through splitDAO, which pays out pending rewards and their ether stake and then burns their tokens.

threats.title: Reentrancy via splitDAO ether payout drains the pool
threats.target: Ether held by the contract / balances[msg.sender] / invariant that ether covers outstanding token balances
threats.approach: An attacker contract buys tokens with createTokenProxy, then calls splitDAO. payOut sends the full token balance in ether through a low-level call that forwards all gas, before balances[msg.sender] and totalSupply are reduced. The attacker's fallback re-enters splitDAO. The balance check still passes, so the attacker is paid its stake again on each recursion, taking other holders' deposited ether until the contract is empty. The burn then runs once per recursion level, which can underflow or leave accounting inconsistent.

threats.title: Reentrancy via reward payout before paidOut update
threats.approach: withdrawRewardFor calls payOut for the reward, and that call forwards all gas before paidOut[msg.sender] is updated. The attacker's fallback re-enters splitDAO or withdrawRewardFor. The entitlement balances*totalRewards/totalSupply minus paidOut is recomputed with the stale paidOut, so the same reward is paid repeatedly. This drains ether that backs other holders' stakes and rewards.

threats.title: Transfer-then-withdraw reward double claim
threats.target: Reward entitlement invariant (balances * totalRewards / totalSupply, paidOut per account)
threats.approach: paidOut is keyed per account, but entitlement depends on the current balance. An attacker claims rewards with account A, then transfers tokens to a fresh account B whose paidOut is 0. B calls splitDAO and claims the full reward on the same tokens again. This repeats across many accounts, and the pool pays more than totalRewards. The tokens are only burned at exit, so the attacker can cycle them through accounts.

threats.title: Reward accounting distorted by supply changes
threats.approach: Entitlement is computed from the current totalSupply and cumulative totalRewards, not from a snapshot at the time rewards arrived. An attacker can deposit a large amount via createTokenProxy just before splitDAO, so that balance/totalSupply is large against the existing totalRewards, and capture rewards that earlier holders accrued. Others' paidOut values and the later burn also change the denominator, so some holders are underpaid and the last withdrawers may find the contract insolvent.

threats.title: tx.origin phishing to seize curator role
threats.approach: changeCurator authorises with tx.origin. An attacker deploys a contract that the curator is lured into calling, for example a fake token or airdrop. In that call the contract invokes changeCurator(attacker). tx.origin equals the curator, so the check passes and the attacker takes the privileged role.

threats.title: Supply/balance desynchronisation through reentrant burn
threats.approach: During the reentrant splitDAO calls, the burn of balances and totalSupply happens after each payout returns. If the arithmetic is unchecked or runs on an older Solidity version, the nested burns subtract the same balance multiple times, which wraps totalSupply or balances[attacker]. This breaks the equality between totalSupply and the sum of balances, and corrupts the reward denominator.

threats.title: Forced ether or rounding breaks solvency accounting
threats.target: Ether solvency invariant / reward share rounding
threats.approach: Integer division in balances*totalRewards/totalSupply rounds down, leaving dust. Ether sent by selfdestruct is not recorded in totalRewards, so it is not distributed and the balance no longer matches the accounting. Users who deposit tiny amounts, or call transfer to split balances, can bias rounding. Because reward payments are taken from the shared pool, any over-payment (see the double claim and reentrancy threats) cuts into the ether backing other holders' stakes.

threats.title: Minting to arbitrary tokenHolder with zero or griefing value
threats.approach: createTokenProxy lets the caller mint to any tokenHolder address. An attacker can mint dust to victim addresses, or to a contract that reverts on receive. When that holder later calls splitDAO, or when the attacker uses the holder to block a flow, the payOut call fails. A holder that is a contract without a payable fallback can lock its own stake. Minting to an address whose paidOut is 0 also gives the attacker fresh accounts to use in reward-claim cycling.

health.headline: 1 critical issue to fix before this goes anywhere near mainnet.

findings.title: Potential Reentrancy Vulnerability
findings.description: Contract uses low-level call with value without reentrancy protection
findings.fix: Import and use OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard modifier on external functions that transfer value

findings.title: Use of tx.origin for Authorization
findings.description: tx.origin should not be used for authorization as it's vulnerable to phishing attacks

findings.title: Floating Pragma
findings.description: Using ^ allows compilation with future compiler versions that may have bugs
findings.fix: Lock pragma to a specific version for production contracts

findings.title: 5 storage slots serialise this contract
findings.description: Every write to these forces the entrypoints touching them into a queue on Monad: totalSupply, totalRewards, curator, balances, paidOut.
findings.fix: Key the state by the caller where the value is theirs, or split a shared counter into stripes that sum back.

findings.title: Shard the counter 'totalSupply'
findings.description: createTokenProxy and splitDAO all increment 'totalSupply', a single slot. Splitting it across N stripes lets N transactions proceed at once; the true value is the sum, read only where it is actually needed. Up to 3 fewer blocked pairs

findings.title: Shard the counter 'totalRewards'
findings.description: receiveReward all increment 'totalRewards', a single slot. Splitting it across N stripes lets N transactions proceed at once; the true value is the sum, read only where it is actually needed. Up to 2 fewer blocked pairs

findings.title: Give 'curator' a key
findings.description: 'curator' is one slot written by changeCurator, and it blocks 1 entrypoint pair. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is. Up to 1 fewer blocked pairs
findings.fix:
mapping(address => address) public curator;

curator[msg.sender] = newValue;

findings.title: 4 functions have no gas bound
findings.description: solc could not bound these, so their cost depends on a loop whose length is decided at runtime and a caller can push them past the block gas limit: createTokenProxy, name, splitDAO, transfer.
findings.fix: Bound the loops, or let callers process a range they choose so the work per transaction is theirs to cap.

findings.title: Gas variance costs real money on Monad
findings.description: Monad debits the sender for the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so anything a wallet pads onto the estimate is spent. solc cannot bound createTokenProxy(address), name(), splitDAO() and 1 more, which is where wallets fall back to a large default limit. Affects monad. Unbounded functions: 4.
findings.fix: Bound the loops, and have your frontend set an explicit gas limit for operations whose cost is fixed rather than letting the wallet estimate and pad.

findings.title: Storage is spread too thinly to amortise Monad's page charge
findings.description: 2 slots across 1 page. Monad pays 8,100 gas for the first touch of each 128-slot page, so slots that sit alone on a page cost more than they would on a per-slot schedule. Summed over the 3 calls traced, that is +17,900 gas. Affects monad. Storage delta: +17,900 gas.
findings.fix: Group state that is read together into a struct so it lands on one page. Each mapping key gets its own page, but a struct stored under that key shares it.

findings.title: State contention will serialise this contract
findings.description: 1 of 5 entrypoints can run concurrently, grade D. 6 of 15 entrypoint pairs always collide, and 3 more collide when they touch the same key, on totalSupply, totalRewards, curator. This only converts into throughput on a chain that executes transactions in parallel. Monad does; every other chain in this comparison executes sequentially, so the same layout buys nothing there and costs nothing either. Affects monad. Colliding entrypoint pairs: 6 of 15.
findings.fix: Key hot state by sender or by id instead of writing to one shared slot. The Parallel Profiler lists the exact pairs and the variables behind them.

findings.title: How long before your app can say the transaction is done
findings.description: Monad reaches deterministic finality in 600 ms, two consensus slots. Base and Arbitrum One confirm through a single sequencer within a couple of seconds, but that confirmation is a promise from the operator; irreversible settlement waits on Ethereum, and a withdrawal waits seven days. Ethereum itself takes about 12.8 minutes. Which number matters depends on what the user is allowed to do next. Affects base, arbitrum. Monad hard finality: 600 ms.

findings.title: Rollups charge for calldata on top of execution gas
findings.description: Base, Arbitrum One publish every transaction's calldata to Ethereum and bill for it separately, and the figures here are execution gas only. The traced calls carry a median of 20 bytes each. Measured against those chains' own fee oracles the omitted charge is fractions of a cent even for a 39 KB deployment, since EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free, so it is a real gap rather than a large one. It moves with Ethereum's fee market, not with your contract. Affects base, arbitrum. Median calldata: 20 B.

findings.title: Monad has no global mempool
findings.description: Transactions are forwarded to the next few block leaders rather than gossiped network-wide, so anything that watches pending transactions works differently. This contract does not appear to depend on pending-transaction visibility, so it is context rather than a change. Affects monad.

chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

caveats: Gas figures come from executing the contract in a local EVM with synthesised arguments. A function guarded by a balance or permission check will revert, and reverted calls are marked rather than counted.
Only state-changing functions are traced. View and pure functions cost nothing to call from outside a transaction.

changes.title: Add errors, reentrancy guard, sharded counters and curator event
changes.why: Adds custom errors, a minimal in-file reentrancy guard, and shards the two hot global counters so different senders stop contending on one slot on Monad. The public getters keep the exact same name, parameters and return type.
fixes: State contention will serialise this contract

changes.title: Expose totalSupply/totalRewards as summing getters plus stripe helper
changes.why: Reconstructs the true totals by summing the stripes; the external interface is unchanged for integrators. The stripe helper keeps the sharding key in one place.

changes.title: Write createTokenProxy into the caller's supply stripe
changes.why: Uses a custom error and increments the per-holder supply stripe instead of the single shared totalSupply slot.

changes.title: Cache balance read and use custom error in transfer
changes.why: Caches the storage read once and uses a custom error; the unchecked subtraction is safe because the balance was just checked.

changes.title: Shard receiveReward into the sender's reward stripe
changes.why: Rewards only ever grow, so a per-sender stripe removes contention on the shared totalRewards slot while the summed getter stays exact.

changes.title: Apply checks-effects-interactions and reentrancy guard to splitDAO
changes.why: Fixes the classic TheDAO reentrancy: the reward is computed first (preserving the exact payout economics), then balance, supply and paidOut are all updated before any ether leaves, and the nonReentrant guard blocks re-entry.

changes.title: Replace tx.origin authorization with msg.sender and emit event
changes.why: Authorizes on msg.sender instead of the phishable tx.origin, uses a custom error, and emits an event for the state change.

contracts.name: TheDAO

health.headline: Nothing critical, and 3 medium severity issues worth a look.

contracts.purpose: A simplified model of The DAO: users deposit ether to mint tokens one-to-one, anyone can add ether as rewards, and a token holder can exit via splitDAO to burn their whole balance and withdraw both their principal and a pro-rata share of rewards. A curator address is stored and can be reassigned by the current curator.

threats.title: Reward accounting ignores paidOut transfer, letting recipients double-claim rewards
threats.target: Invariant: pending reward = max(0, balance*totalRewards/totalSupply - paidOut); reward pool ether
threats.approach: paidOut is keyed to the account, not to tokens. An attacker with a large balance calls splitDAO to collect the reward, then moves ether to a fresh address and mints tokens again. The fresh address has paidOut = 0 and a new balance, so it claims a pro-rata share of the same totalRewards. Because totalRewards never decreases and totalSupply drops after the burn, the ratio balance*totalRewards/totalSupply grows. Repeating this drains ether that backs other holders' principal.

threats.title: Transfer-based reward laundering: tokens moved to a clean address with paidOut=0
threats.target: Invariant: paidOut[account] accumulates reward already paid; balances only change via transfer/mint/split
threats.approach: A holder who has already collected rewards, or has high paidOut, transfers tokens to a fresh address with paidOut = 0. The new address calls splitDAO and receives the full cumulative reward share balance*totalRewards/totalSupply. Several colluding addresses can each claim rewards that were attributed to the same tokens before the transfer. The attacker can also do the reverse: moving tokens away from an address with high paidOut.

threats.title: Reentrancy into transfer/createTokenProxy/receiveReward during splitDAO payout callbacks
threats.target: Invariant: splitDAO state changes precede payouts; _locked guards only splitDAO
threats.approach: The reward call forwards all gas to msg.sender. The lock covers only splitDAO. A malicious contract receiving the reward call can call transfer, createTokenProxy or receiveReward. Balance is already zeroed and supply reduced, but totalRewards can be inflated, or the attacker can mint tokens and move them to a second address mid-execution. That second address then splits with an inconsistent totalSupply/totalRewards ratio, so the reward and principal calculations use manipulated values.

threats.title: Supply/rewards ratio manipulation via striped totals and mod-16 stripes
threats.target: Invariant: totalSupply is the sum of signed stripe deltas; stripe = address mod 16
threats.approach: The attacker picks addresses whose stripe differs from the holders' stripes. Burning in splitDAO subtracts from the caller's stripe, which can push it negative. Reading totalSupply or totalRewards while it is mid-update, or choosing which stripe to mint into, changes none of the sums but shifts accounting unexpectedly if the sum has rounding or underflow. With signed deltas, an implementation error would make totalSupply wrong, for instance zero or negative, causing division by zero (a DoS on all splits) or inflated reward ratios.

threats.title: Principal paid after reward may exceed contract solvency, so last exiters are stuck
threats.target: Asset: ether held vs. token balances; invariant that splitDAO reverts on payout failure
threats.approach: Rewards are paid from the same ether pool as deposits, and the reward formula can overpay early claimants (see double-claim). Principal for later holders then exceeds the contract balance, so their splitDAO call reverts on a failed payout call. Their tokens become unredeemable. An attacker can also deliberately front-run exits to drain the pool.

threats.title: Griefing via payout revert or gas-consuming receiver
threats.target: Invariant: splitDAO reverts if payout fails; user funds liveness
threats.approach: A holder who is a contract can be made to fail payout, for example by an attacker minting tokens to a contract address that rejects ether, or by sending tokens via transfer to such a contract. Those tokens can never be split. They still count in totalSupply, so they dilute rewards for others and permanently lock their share of the ether.

threats.title: Dust or rounding exploitation in the reward formula
threats.target: Invariant: pending reward = max(0, balance*totalRewards/totalSupply - paidOut)
threats.approach: The attacker mints a tiny balance relative to a large totalSupply, or times calls after the supply shrinks. Integer division rounding then pays slightly more than fair on repeated small accounts. Splitting the attacker's holdings across many addresses, each with paidOut = 0, collects rounding gains. If totalSupply is 0 after the last holder splits while totalRewards > 0, the reward calculation divides by zero, which breaks later interactions.

threats.title: Curator takeover or loss
threats.target: Invariant: only the current curator can change the curator; curator role
threats.approach: The curator role has no timelock or two-step transfer. If the curator key is compromised, or changeCurator is called with a wrong or zero address, the role is lost or captured permanently. The curator has no direct fund-moving power in the listed functions, so the impact is limited to governance and privilege capture.

threats.title: Minting tokens to arbitrary holders enabling unsolicited positions and reward dilution
threats.target: Invariant: balances only increase via createTokenProxy or incoming transfer; token balances as claims
threats.approach: createTokenProxy lets any caller credit tokens to a chosen address. An attacker can mint tiny balances to a victim contract, or a large balance to a controlled address just after receiveReward. This raises totalSupply and dilutes the pro-rata share of existing holders. The attacker then splits and recovers principal plus a reward share computed against rewards that arrived before they deposited, a reward-sniping attack.

findings.description: solc could not bound these, so their cost depends on a loop whose length is decided at runtime and a caller can push them past the block gas limit: createTokenProxy, name, receiveReward, splitDAO, totalRewards, totalSupply, transfer.

findings.fix: Bound the loops, and have your frontend set an explicit gas limit for operations whose cost is fixed rather than letting the wallet estimate and pad.
findings.title: Gas variance costs real money on Monad
findings.description: Monad debits the sender for the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so anything a wallet pads onto the estimate is spent. solc cannot bound createTokenProxy(address), name(), receiveReward() and 4 more, which is where wallets fall back to a large default limit. Affects monad. Unbounded functions: 7.

findings.fix: Group state that is read together into a struct so it lands on one page. Each mapping key gets its own page, but a struct stored under that key shares it.
findings.title: Storage is spread too thinly to amortise Monad's page charge
findings.description: 3 slots across 2 pages. Monad pays 8,100 gas for the first touch of each 128-slot page, so slots that sit alone on a page cost more than they would on a per-slot schedule. Summed over the 3 calls traced, that is +12,900 gas. Affects monad. Storage delta: +12,900 gas.

findings.title: Contract is shaped for parallel execution
findings.description: 3 of 5 entrypoints can run concurrently, grade B. 2 of 15 entrypoint pairs always collide, and 7 more collide when they touch the same key, on _locked, curator, balances. This only converts into throughput on a chain that executes transactions in parallel. Monad does; every other chain in this comparison executes sequentially, so the same layout buys nothing there and costs nothing either. Colliding entrypoint pairs: 2 of 15.

findings.title: How long before your app can say the transaction is done
findings.description: Monad reaches deterministic finality in 600 ms, two consensus slots. Base and Arbitrum One confirm through a single sequencer within a couple of seconds, but that confirmation is a promise from the operator; irreversible settlement waits on Ethereum, and a withdrawal waits seven days. Ethereum itself takes about 12.8 minutes. Which number matters depends on what the user is allowed to do next. Affects base, arbitrum. Monad hard finality: 600 ms.

findings.title: Rollups charge for calldata on top of execution gas
findings.description: Base, Arbitrum One publish every transaction's calldata to Ethereum and bill for it separately, and the figures here are execution gas only. The traced calls carry a median of 20 bytes each. Measured against those chains' own fee oracles the omitted charge is fractions of a cent even for a 39 KB deployment, since EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free, so it is a real gap rather than a large one. It moves with Ethereum's fee market, not with your contract. Affects base, arbitrum. Median calldata: 20 B.

findings.title: Monad has no global mempool
findings.description: Transactions are forwarded to the next few block leaders rather than gossiped network-wide, so anything that watches pending transactions works differently. This contract does not appear to depend on pending-transaction visibility, so it is context rather than a change. Affects monad.

chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

Gas figures come from executing the contract in a local EVM with synthesised arguments. A function guarded by a balance or permission check will revert, and reverted calls are marked rather than counted.
Only state-changing functions are traced. View and pure functions cost nothing to call from outside a transaction.

Only execution and intrinsic gas is modelled. Rollups additionally charge for publishing calldata to Ethereum, which is not included. Measured against the live oracles, that fee is around $0.0001 on Base and $0.00002 on Arbitrum even for a 39 KB deployment, three to four orders of magnitude below the execution cost shown, because EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free.
Ethereum storage cost is measured from the EVM. The Monad figure is that measurement adjusted by the published MIP-8 schedule.

parallel.summary: State is well separated. Most transactions against this contract can execute concurrently on Monad. 2 slots are shared by every caller: _locked and curator. Any two transactions that touch one of them serialise. splitDAO() and changeCurator() cannot run alongside each other. 2 view functions were excluded: they send no transactions and never contend.

suggestions.title: Give '_locked' a key
suggestions.description: '_locked' is one slot written by splitDAO, and it blocks 1 entrypoint pair. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is.

suggestions.title: Give 'curator' a key
suggestions.description: 'curator' is one slot written by changeCurator, and it blocks 1 entrypoint pair. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is.

mapping(address => address) public curator;

curator[msg.sender] = newValue;
